case_info.scenario: A 71-year-old woman without substantial medical history was referred for 2 months of progressive worsening of vision and pain in her right eye despite corticosteroid treatment following a recent excisional conjunctival biopsy with cryotherapy at an outside institution for suspected squamous cell carcinoma in situ. Pathology was reported to be negative for malignancy. The patient noted postoperative pain that was suspected to be postsurgical inflammatory scleritis and managed by an outside ophthalmologist with a combination of topical prednisolone, oral prednisone, and subtenon triamcinolone acetonide. On presentation, the patient’s Snellen visual acuity without correction was count fingers in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye with a baseline of 20/100 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye. The anterior segment examination of the right eye revealed conjunctival hyperemia with prominent scleral vessels, greatest inferiorly. Scleral thinning was noted inferotemporally, as well as a temporal crescent of corneal stromal melt (Figure 1). A persistent depot of subtenon triamcinolone acetonide was noted inferotemporally. A retrocorneal white plaque was noted from clock positions 6:00 to 9:30 with 4+ cell and flare per Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature classification. Posterior synechiae were present and the pupil was peaked inferotemporally. There was no view posteriorly and a B-scan ultrasonography revealed moderate vitreous opacities without retinal detachment, choroidal effusion, or Tenon space edema. The left eye was normal.

case_info.explanation: Nocardiascleritis with anterior chamber inflammation C. Perform anterior chamber biopsy of retrocorneal plaque The patient’s postoperative worsening and development of retrocorneal plaque following courses of topical, periocular, and oral corticosteroids by the referring eye care professionals were concerning for an infectious etiology. Given the substantial worsening with corticosteroid treatment and the characteristic retrocorneal plaque, infectious etiologies likeNocardiashould be ruled out with anterior chamber biopsy (choice C). The appearance is atypical for vitreoretinal lymphoma and empirically injecting intravitreal methotrexate without tissue diagnosis is not recommended (choice A). The benign pathology report and retrocorneal plaque are atypical of ocular surface squamous neoplasia and topical interferon alpha-2b would be inappropriate (choice B). Anterior chamber culture is preferred with a predominant anterior chamber infiltrate and B-scan ultrasonography without substantial vitritis. If intravitreal injections were chosen as initial management, intravitreal amikacin should be included because of high suspicion forNocardia(choice D). An in-office anterior chamber tap was unsuccessful due to the retrocorneal plaque thickness. Surgical biopsy was performed with a 25-gauge vitrectomy cutter connected to a 5-mL syringe the following day. A 25-gauge needle and anterior chamber cannula were unsuccessful in aspirating the material intraoperatively. Intravitreal amikacin, vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole were administered and oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was started immediately. Once biopsy results confirmedNocardia cyriacigeorgica, topical amikacin (2.5%) and linezolid (0.2%) were started. Nocardiaaccounts for 8% of reported cases of infectious scleritis and frequently remains an indolent infection.1,2It is rarely seen in patients with immunocompetence except in substantial ocular trauma wherein it presents with anterior segment inflammation, hypopyon, and anterior vitreous and surgical site exudates.3In this case, the potential for nosocomial introduction from surgical trauma and corticosteroid use necessitates consideration ofNocardia.4﻿Nocardiamay be mistaken for other bacterial or fungal pathogens due to the presence of anterior chamber exudates on the corneal epithelium.5,6Antibiotic choice must be considered as aggregate susceptibility testing recognizesNocardiaas highly susceptible to amikacin but resistant to vancomycin.5Patients typically require prolonged systemic and topical antibiotics for complete resolution.7 Visual prognosis is usually poor, but is linked to presenting visual acuity and duration of infection.5,8,9Superior visual outcomes in cases ofNocardiaendophthalmitis are associated with male sex, presenting vision better than hand motions, presentation within 48 hours of symptoms onset, and initial intervention being vitrectomy instead of vitreous biopsy.5 Our case presents a patient with immunocompetence whose disease course worsened after corticosteroid use. The proliferation ofNocardiawas perhaps associated with cryotherapy following conjunctival biopsy which is otherwise associated with improved outcomes.10﻿Nocardiaendophthalmitis is rare, but a retrocorneal plaque should raise clinical suspicion to ensure prompt treatment with sufficient antibiotic coverage and avoid long-term visual deficits or enucleation. The patient noted substantial resolution of pain and improvement in visual acuity with stabilization of scleral thinning and resolution of the retrocorneal plaque (Figure 2). Best-corrected Snellen visual acuity remains count fingers in the right eye due to a dense cataract.

dialogue_history.text: I disagree with proceeding directly to intravitreal antibiotics and antifungals. This presentation—worsening despite steroids, scleral thinning, corneal melt, and a retrocorneal plaque adjacent to a steroid depot—is highly suggestive of infectious scleritis or keratoscleritis, possibly fungal or atypical bacterial, not typical endophthalmitis. The immediate step should be a targeted diagnostic workup, such as cultures from the plaque or scleral melt site, before empiric intravitreal therapy, which could delay identifying the specific pathogen.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.

       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

     message.

   Scoring:

       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

A 71-year-old woman without substantial medical history was referred for 2 months of progressive worsening of vision and pain in her right eye despite corticosteroid treatment following a recent excisional conjunctival biopsy with cryotherapy at an outside institution for suspected squamous cell carcinoma in situ. The patient noted postoperative pain that was suspected to be postsurgical inflammatory scleritis and managed by an outside ophthalmologist with a combination of topical prednisolone, oral prednisone, and subtenon triamcinolone acetonide. On presentation, the patient’s Snellen visual acuity without correction was count fingers in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye with a baseline of 20/100 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye. The anterior segment examination of the right eye revealed conjunctival hyperemia with prominent scleral vessels, greatest inferiorly. Scleral thinning was noted inferotemporally, as well as a temporal crescent of corneal stromal melt (Figure 1). A persistent depot of subtenon triamcinolone acetonide was noted inferotemporally. A retrocorneal white plaque was noted from clock positions 6:00 to 9:30 with 4+ cell and flare per Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature classification. Posterior synechiae were present and the pupil was peaked inferotemporally. There was no view posteriorly and a B-scan ultrasonography revealed moderate vitreous opacities without retinal detachment, choroidal effusion, or Tenon space edema. The left eye was normal.

Perform anterior chamber biopsy of retrocorneal plaque The patient’s postoperative worsening and development of retrocorneal plaque following courses of topical, periocular, and oral corticosteroids by the referring eye care professionals were concerning for an infectious etiology. Anterior chamber culture is preferred with a predominant anterior chamber infiltrate and B-scan ultrasonography without substantial vitritis. An in-office anterior chamber tap was unsuccessful due to the retrocorneal plaque thickness. Surgical biopsy was performed with a 25-gauge vitrectomy cutter connected to a 5-mL syringe the following day. A 25-gauge needle and anterior chamber cannula were unsuccessful in aspirating the material intraoperatively. Intravitreal amikacin, vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole were administered and oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was started immediately. Once biopsy results confirmedNocardia cyriacigeorgica, topical amikacin (2.5%) and linezolid (0.2%) were started. Nocardiaaccounts for 8% of reported cases of infectious scleritis and frequently remains an indolent infection.1,2It is rarely seen in patients with immunocompetence except in substantial ocular trauma wherein it presents with anterior segment inflammation, hypopyon, and anterior vitreous and surgical site exudates.3In this case, the potential for nosocomial introduction from surgical trauma and corticosteroid use necessitates consideration ofNocardia.4﻿Nocardiamay be mistaken for other bacterial or fungal pathogens due to the presence of anterior chamber exudates on the corneal epithelium.5,6Antibiotic choice must be considered as aggregate susceptibility testing recognizesNocardiaas highly susceptible to amikacin but resistant to vancomycin.5Patients typically require prolonged systemic and topical antibiotics for complete resolution.7 Visual prognosis is usually poor, but is linked to presenting visual acuity and duration of infection.5,8,9Superior visual outcomes in cases ofNocardiaendophthalmitis are associated with male sex, presenting vision better than hand motions, presentation within 48 hours of symptoms onset, and initial intervention being vitrectomy instead of vitreous biopsy.5 Our case presents a patient with immunocompetence whose disease course worsened after corticosteroid use. The proliferation ofNocardiawas perhaps associated with cryotherapy following conjunctival biopsy which is otherwise associated with improved outcomes.10﻿Nocardiaendophthalmitis is rare, but a retrocorneal plaque should raise clinical suspicion to ensure prompt treatment with sufficient antibiotic coverage and avoid long-term visual deficits or enucleation. The patient noted substantial resolution of pain and improvement in visual acuity with stabilization of scleral thinning and resolution of the retrocorneal plaque (Figure 2). [NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration

case_info.explanation: Nocardiascleritis with anterior chamber inflammation C. Perform anterior chamber biopsy of retrocorneal plaque The patient’s postoperative worsening and development of retrocorneal plaque following courses of topical, periocular, and oral corticosteroids by the referring eye care professionals were concerning for an infectious etiology. Given the substantial worsening with corticosteroid treatment and the characteristic retrocorneal plaque, infectious etiologies likeNocardiashould be ruled out with anterior chamber biopsy (choice C). The appearance is atypical for vitreoretinal lymphoma and empirically injecting intravitreal methotrexate without tissue diagnosis is not recommended (choice A). The benign pathology report and retrocorneal plaque are atypical of ocular surface squamous neoplasia and topical interferon alpha-2b would be inappropriate (choice B). Anterior chamber culture is preferred with a predominant anterior chamber infiltrate and B-scan ultrasonography without substantial vitritis. If intravitreal injections were chosen as initial management, intravitreal amikacin should be included because of high suspicion forNocardia(choice D). An in-office anterior chamber tap was unsuccessful due to the retrocorneal plaque thickness. Surgical biopsy was performed with a 25-gauge vitrectomy cutter connected to a 5-mL syringe the following day. A 25-gauge needle and anterior chamber cannula were unsuccessful in aspirating the material intraoperatively. Intravitreal amikacin, vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole were administered and oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was started immediately. Once biopsy results confirmedNocardia cyriacigeorgica, topical amikacin (2.5%) and linezolid (0.2%) were started. Nocardiaaccounts for 8% of reported cases of infectious scleritis and frequently remains an indolent infection.1,2It is rarely seen in patients with immunocompetence except in substantial ocular trauma wherein it presents with anterior segment inflammation, hypopyon, and anterior vitreous and surgical site exudates.3In this case, the potential for nosocomial introduction from surgical trauma and corticosteroid use necessitates consideration ofNocardia.4﻿Nocardiamay be mistaken for other bacterial or fungal pathogens due to the presence of anterior chamber exudates on the corneal epithelium.5,6Antibiotic choice must be considered as aggregate susceptibility testing recognizesNocardiaas highly susceptible to amikacin but resistant to vancomycin.5Patients typically require prolonged systemic and topical antibiotics for complete resolution.7 Visual prognosis is usually poor, but is linked to presenting visual acuity and duration of infection.5,8,9Superior visual outcomes in cases ofNocardiaendophthalmitis are associated with male sex, presenting vision better than hand motions, presentation within 48 hours of symptoms onset, and initial intervention being vitrectomy instead of vitreous biopsy.5 Our case presents a patient with immunocompetence whose disease course worsened after corticosteroid use. The proliferation ofNocardiawas perhaps associated with cryotherapy following conjunctival biopsy which is otherwise associated with improved outcomes.10﻿Nocardiaendophthalmitis is rare, but a retrocorneal plaque should raise clinical suspicion to ensure prompt treatment with sufficient antibiotic coverage and avoid long-term visual deficits or enucleation. The patient noted substantial resolution of pain and improvement in visual acuity with stabilization of scleral thinning and resolution of the retrocorneal plaque (Figure 2). Best-corrected Snellen visual acuity remains count fingers in the right eye due to a dense cataract.

case_info.explanation: Nocardiascleritis with anterior chamber inflammation C. Perform anterior chamber biopsy of retrocorneal plaque The patient’s postoperative worsening and development of retrocorneal plaque following courses of topical, periocular, and oral corticosteroids by the referring eye care professionals were concerning for an infectious etiology. Given the substantial worsening with corticosteroid treatment and the characteristic retrocorneal plaque, infectious etiologies likeNocardiashould be ruled out with anterior chamber biopsy (choice C). The appearance is atypical for vitreoretinal lymphoma and empirically injecting intravitreal methotrexate without tissue diagnosis is not recommended (choice A). The benign pathology report and retrocorneal plaque are atypical of ocular surface squamous neoplasia and topical interferon alpha-2b would be inappropriate (choice B). Anterior chamber culture is preferred with a predominant anterior chamber infiltrate and B-scan ultrasonography without substantial vitritis. If intravitreal injections were chosen as initial management, intravitreal amikacin should be included because of high suspicion forNocardia(choice D). An in-office anterior chamber tap was unsuccessful due to the retrocorneal plaque thickness. Surgical biopsy was performed with a 25-gauge vitrectomy cutter connected to a 5-mL syringe the following day. A 25-gauge needle and anterior chamber cannula were unsuccessful in aspirating the material intraoperatively. Intravitreal amikacin, vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole were administered and oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was started immediately. case_info.explanation: Nocardiascleritis with anterior chamber inflammation C. Perform anterior chamber biopsy of retrocorneal plaque The patient’s postoperative worsening and development of retrocorneal plaque following courses of topical, periocular, and oral corticosteroids by the referring eye care professionals were concerning for an infectious etiology. Given the substantial worsening with corticosteroid treatment and the characteristic retrocorneal plaque, infectious etiologies likeNocardiashould be ruled out with anterior chamber biopsy (choice C). The appearance is atypical for vitreoretinal lymphoma and empirically injecting intravitreal methotrexate without tissue diagnosis is not recommended (choice A). The benign pathology report and retrocorneal plaque are atypical of ocular surface squamous neoplasia and topical interferon alpha-2b would be inappropriate (choice B). Anterior chamber culture is preferred with a predominant anterior chamber infiltrate and B-scan ultrasonography without substantial vitritis. If intravitreal injections were chosen as initial management, intravitreal amikacin should be included because of high suspicion forNocardia(choice D). An in-office anterior chamber tap was unsuccessful due to the retrocorneal plaque thickness. Surgical biopsy was performed with a 25-gauge vitrectomy cutter connected to a 5-mL syringe the following day. A 25-gauge needle and anterior chamber cannula were unsuccessful in aspirating the material intraoperatively. Intravitreal amikacin, vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole were administered and oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was started immediately. Once biopsy results confirmedNocardia cyriacigeorgica, topical amikacin (2.5%) and linezolid (0.2%) were started. Nocardiaaccounts for 8% of reported cases of infectious scleritis and frequently remains an indolent infection.1,2It is rarely seen in patients with immunocompetence except in substantial ocular trauma wherein it presents with anterior segment inflammation, hypopyon, and anterior vitreous and surgical site exudates.3In this case, the potential for nosocomial introduction from surgical trauma and corticosteroid use necessitates consideration ofNocardia.4﻿Nocardiamay be mistaken for other bacterial or fungal pathogens due to the presence of anterior chamber exudates on the corneal epithelium.5,6Antibiotic choice must be considered as aggregate susceptibility testing recognizesNocardiaas highly susceptible to amikacin but resistant to vancomycin.5Patients typically require prolonged systemic and topical antibiotics for complete resolution.7 Visual prognosis is usually poor, but is linked to presenting visual acuity and duration of infection.5,8,9Superior visual outcomes in cases ofNocardiaendophthalmitis are associated with male sex, presenting vision better than hand motions, presentation within 48 hours of symptoms onset, and initial intervention being vitrectomy instead of vitreous biopsy.5 Our case presents a patient with immunocompetence whose disease course worsened after corticosteroid use. The proliferation ofNocardiawas perhaps associated with cryotherapy following conjunctival biopsy which is otherwise associated with improved outcomes.10﻿Nocardiaendophthalmitis is rare, but a retrocorneal plaque should raise clinical suspicion to ensure prompt treatment with sufficient antibiotic coverage and avoid long-term visual deficits or enucleation. The patient noted substantial resolution of pain and improvement in visual acuity with stabilization of scleral thinning and resolution of the retrocorneal plaque (Figure 2). Best-corrected Snellen visual acuity remains count fingers in the right eye due to a dense cataract.

case_info.explanation: Nocardiascleritis with anterior chamber inflammation C. Perform anterior chamber biopsy of retrocorneal plaque The patient’s postoperative worsening and development of retrocorneal plaque following courses of topical, periocular, and oral corticosteroids by the referring eye care professionals were concerning for an infectious etiology. Given the substantial worsening with corticosteroid treatment and the characteristic retrocorneal plaque, infectious etiologies likeNocardiashould be ruled out with anterior chamber biopsy (choice C). The appearance is atypical for vitreoretinal lymphoma and empirically injecting intravitreal methotrexate without tissue diagnosis is not recommended (choice A). The benign pathology report and retrocorneal plaque are atypical of ocular surface squamous neoplasia and topical interferon alpha-2b would be inappropriate (choice B). Anterior chamber culture is preferred with a predominant anterior chamber infiltrate and B-scan ultrasonography without substantial vitritis. If intravitreal injections were chosen as initial management, intravitreal amikacin should be included because of high suspicion forNocardia(choice D). An in-office anterior chamber tap was unsuccessful due to the retrocorneal plaque thickness. Surgical biopsy was performed with a 25-gauge vitrectomy cutter connected to a 5-mL syringe the following day. A 25-gauge needle and anterior chamber cannula were unsuccessful in aspirating the material intraoperatively. Intravitreal amikacin, vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole were administered and oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was started immediately. Once biopsy results confirmedNocardia cyriacigeorgica, topical amikacin (2.5%) and linezolid (0.2%) were started. Nocardiaaccounts for 8% of reported cases of infectious scleritis and frequently remains an indolent infection.1,2It is rarely seen in patients with immunocompetence except in substantial ocular trauma wherein it presents with anterior segment inflammation, hypopyon, and anterior vitreous and surgical site exudates.3In this case, the potential for nosocomial introduction from surgical trauma and corticosteroid use necessitates consideration ofNocardia.4﻿Nocardiamay be mistaken for other bacterial or fungal pathogens due to the presence of anterior chamber exudates on the corneal epithelium.5,6Antibiotic choice must be considered as aggregate susceptibility testing recognizesNocardiaas highly susceptible to amikacin but resistant to vancomycin.5Patients typically require prolonged systemic and topical antibiotics for complete resolution.7 Visual prognosis is usually poor, but is linked to presenting visual acuity and duration of infection.5,8,9Superior visual outcomes in cases ofNocardiaendophthalmitis are associated with male sex, presenting vision better than hand motions, presentation within 48 hours of symptoms onset, and initial intervention being vitrectomy instead of vitreous biopsy.5 Our case presents a patient with immunocompetence whose disease course worsened after corticosteroid use. The proliferation ofNocardiawas perhaps associated with cryotherapy following conjunctival biopsy which is otherwise associated with improved outcomes.10﻿Nocardiaendophthalmitis is rare, but a retrocorneal plaque should raise clinical suspicion to ensure prompt treatment with sufficient antibiotic coverage and avoid long-term visual deficits or enucleation. The patient noted substantial resolution of pain and improvement in visual acuity with stabilization of scleral thinning and resolution of the retrocorneal plaque (Figure 2). Best-corrected Snellen visual acuity remains count fingers in the right eye due to a dense cataract.

case_info.explanation: Nocardiascleritis with anterior chamber inflammation C. Perform anterior chamber biopsy of retrocorneal plaque The patient’s postoperative worsening and development of retrocorneal plaque following courses of topical, periocular, and oral corticosteroids by the referring eye care professionals were concerning for an infectious etiology. Given the substantial worsening with corticosteroid treatment and the characteristic retrocorneal plaque, infectious etiologies likeNocardiashould be ruled out with anterior chamber biopsy (choice C). The appearance is atypical for vitreoretinal lymphoma and empirically injecting intravitreal methotrexate without tissue diagnosis is not recommended (choice A). The benign pathology report and retrocorneal plaque are atypical of ocular surface squamous neoplasia and topical interferon alpha-2b would be inappropriate (choice B). Anterior chamber culture is preferred with a predominant anterior chamber infiltrate and B-scan ultrasonography without substantial vitritis. If intravitreal injections were chosen as initial management, intravitreal amikacin should be included because of high suspicion forNocardia(choice D). An in-office anterior chamber tap was unsuccessful due to the retrocorneal plaque thickness. Surgical biopsy was performed with a 25-gauge vitrectomy cutter connected to a 5-mL syringe the following day. A 25-gauge needle and anterior chamber cannula were unsuccessful in aspirating the material intraoperatively. Intravitreal amikacin, vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole were administered and oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was started immediately. Once biopsy results confirmedNocardia cyriacigeorgica, topical amikacin (2.5%) and linezolid (0.2%) were started. Nocardiaaccounts for 8% of reported cases of infectious scleritis and frequently remains an indolent infection.1,2It is rarely seen in patients with immunocompetence except in substantial ocular trauma wherein it presents with anterior segment inflammation, hypopyon, and anterior vitreous and surgical site exudates.3In this case, the potential for nosocomial introduction from surgical trauma and corticosteroid use necessitates consideration ofNocardia.4﻿Nocardiamay be mistaken for other bacterial or fungal pathogens due to the presence of anterior chamber exudates on the corneal epithelium.5,6Antibiotic choice must be considered as aggregate susceptibility testing recognizesNocardiaas highly susceptible to amikacin but resistant to vancomycin.5Patients typically require prolonged systemic and topical antibiotics for complete resolution.7 Visual prognosis is usually poor, but is linked to presenting visual acuity and duration of infection.5,8,9Superior visual outcomes in cases ofNocardiaendophthalmitis are associated with male sex, presenting vision better than hand motions, presentation within 48 hours of symptoms onset, and initial intervention being vitrectomy instead of vitreous biopsy.5 Our case presents a patient with immunocompetence whose disease course worsened after corticosteroid use. The proliferation ofNocardiawas perhaps associated with cryotherapy following conjunctival biopsy which is otherwise associated with improved outcomes.10﻿Nocardiaendophthalmitis is rare, but a retrocorneal plaque should raise clinical suspicion to ensure prompt treatment with sufficient antibiotic coverage and avoid long-term visual deficits or enucleation. The patient noted substantial resolution of pain and improvement in visual acuity with stabilization of scleral thinning and resolution of the retrocorneal plaque (Figure 2). Best-corrected Snellen visual acuity remains count fingers in the right eye due to a dense cataract.

case_info.explanation: Nocardiascleritis with anterior chamber inflammation C. Perform anterior chamber biopsy of retrocorneal plaque The patient’s postoperative worsening and development of retrocorneal plaque following courses of topical, periocular, and oral corticosteroids by the referring eye care professionals were concerning for an infectious etiology. Given the substantial worsening with corticosteroid treatment and the characteristic retrocorneal plaque, infectious etiologies likeNocardiashould be ruled out with anterior chamber biopsy (choice C). The appearance is atypical for vitreoretinal lymphoma and empirically injecting intravitreal methotrexate without tissue diagnosis is not recommended (choice A). The benign pathology report and retrocorneal plaque are atypical of ocular surface squamous neoplasia and topical interferon alpha-2b would be inappropriate (choice B). Anterior chamber culture is preferred with a predominant anterior chamber infiltrate and B-scan ultrasonography without substantial vitritis. If intravitreal injections were chosen as initial management, intravitreal amikacin should be included because of high suspicion forNocardia(choice D). An in-office anterior chamber tap was unsuccessful due to the retrocorneal plaque thickness. Surgical biopsy was performed with a 25-gauge vitrectomy cutter connected to a 5-mL syringe the following day. A 25-gauge needle and anterior chamber cannula were unsuccessful in aspirating the material intraoperatively. Intravitreal amikacin, vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole were administered and oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was started immediately. Once biopsy results confirmedNocardia cyriacigeorgica, topical amikacin (2.5%) and linezolid (0.2%) were started. Nocardiaaccounts for 8% of reported cases of infectious scleritis and frequently remains an indolent infection.1,2It is rarely seen in patients with immunocompetence except in substantial ocular trauma wherein it presents with anterior segment inflammation, hypopyon, and anterior vitreous and surgical site exudates.3In this case, the potential for nosocomial introduction from surgical trauma and corticosteroid use necessitates consideration ofNocardia.4﻿Nocardiamay be mistaken for other bacterial or fungal pathogens due to the presence of anterior chamber exudates on the corneal epithelium.5,6Antibiotic choice must be considered as aggregate susceptibility testing recognizesNocardiaas highly susceptible to amikacin but resistant to vancomycin.5Patients typically require prolonged systemic and topical antibiotics for complete resolution.7 Visual prognosis is usually poor, but is linked to presenting visual acuity and duration of infection.5,8,9Superior visual outcomes in cases ofNocardiaendophthalmitis are associated with male sex, presenting vision better than hand motions, presentation within 48 hours of symptoms onset, and initial intervention being vitrectomy instead of vitreous biopsy.5 Our case presents a patient with immunocompetence whose disease course worsened after corticosteroid use. The proliferation ofNocardiawas perhaps associated with cryotherapy following conjunctival biopsy which is otherwise associated with improved outcomes.10﻿Nocardiaendophthalmitis is rare, but a retrocorneal plaque should raise clinical suspicion to ensure prompt treatment with sufficient antibiotic coverage and avoid long-term visual deficits or enucleation. The patient noted substantial resolution of pain and improvement in visual acuity with stabilization of scleral thinning and resolution of the retrocorneal plaque (Figure 2). Best-corrected Snellen visual acuity remains count fingers in the right eye due to a dense cataract.
